name: CDN
intent: Serve static content from servers close to the user, so far-away visitors do not pay for a long round trip to your origin.
scenario: A website stores its images and scripts on one origin server in the US. Visitors in Europe and Asia wait much longer for every file than visitors next to the server.
problem: Distance costs time. Light in fibre is fast, but a request to a server on the other side of the world still takes hundreds of milliseconds, and a page needs dozens of requests. Every user also hits your single origin for the same unchanging files, which wastes its bandwidth and capacity.

howItWorks.title: Users are routed to a nearby edge
howItWorks.text: A content delivery network runs many points of presence (edge servers) around the world. DNS or anycast routing (one address announced from many places) sends each user to the closest healthy one.

howItWorks.title: A hit is served from the edge
howItWorks.text: If the edge already has a fresh copy of the file, it answers immediately. The request never reaches your origin.

howItWorks.title: A miss fetches from the origin once
howItWorks.text: On the first request, the edge asks the origin, returns the file to the user, and keeps a copy according to the Cache-Control headers. Everyone after that, nearby, gets a hit.

howItWorks.title: Freshness is controlled by TTLs, purges and versioned URLs
howItWorks.text: A TTL (time to live) decides how long an edge may reuse a copy. A purge removes a file early. Many sites avoid purging by putting a hash in the file name (app.3f9a1c.js), so a new version is simply a new URL.

howItWorks.title: The edge does more than cache
howItWorks.text: It terminates TLS close to the user, compresses files, absorbs traffic spikes and some attacks, and can run small pieces of code at the edge.

pros: Much lower latency for distant users
Offloads bandwidth and requests from your origin
Absorbs traffic spikes and some denial-of-service attacks
Usually cheap and easy to add in front of a site
cons: Stale content until the TTL expires or you purge
Little benefit for personalised or constantly changing responses
Cache configuration mistakes can leak private data or serve the wrong version
Another vendor and another layer to debug
whenToUse: Static assets: images, video, scripts, styles, downloads
Public pages that change rarely or can be a little stale
whenNotToUse: All your users are in one region, close to the origin
Responses are unique per user and cannot be cached
Content must be instantly consistent everywhere
pitfalls: Caching a personalised response and showing it to other users
Forgetting that a purge takes time to reach every edge
Ignoring the origin: a miss storm after a purge can overwhelm it
Using the same URL for new content, so users keep seeing the old file

roles.label: User
roles.description: A visitor somewhere in the world.

roles.label: Edge server
roles.description: A nearby cache that serves the file or fetches it.

quiz.question: A site serves /static/app.js with a one-year cache lifetime. After a deploy, many users still run the old script. What is the best fix?
options: Purge /static/app.js on the CDN after every deploy, so edge copies are removed and refetched.
Put a content hash in the file name, such as app.3f9a1c.js, so each version has a new URL.
Cut the lifetime to 60 seconds for all static files, so any stale copy expires quickly.
Add a second CDN in front of the first one, so the request goes to the nearest fresh copy.
quiz.explanation: A new URL cannot be served stale by the edge or by browsers, and needs no purge. A purge does not reach copies in browsers, a short lifetime throws away most of the benefit of caching, and a second CDN in front only adds another cache with the same stale copy.

quiz.question: An /api/me endpoint returns the signed-in user's name. It is sent with Cache-Control: public, max-age=300 and sits behind a CDN. Users report seeing other people's names. What is the right fix?
options: Lower max-age to 5 seconds, so a wrong name can only be shown for a very short time.
Purge the CDN every minute, so nobody keeps a copy of another user's page for long.
Mark personalised responses private or no-store, and cache only the shared parts.
Add edge locations nearer the users, so each region has fewer people sharing a copy.
quiz.explanation: The edge treats a public response as one copy for everyone. A shorter lifetime or frequent purges still show private data to others, only for less time. More edge locations do not change that each public copy is shared by everyone it serves.

quiz.question: After a rebrand, a team purges the whole 2 TB image catalogue from the CDN at once. Edge caches go cold and the origin falls over under the refetch. Next time, what is the better plan?
options: Purge everything at once again but add ten times the origin servers
Set the cache lifetime to zero, so the edge always checks and no cold start can happen.
Purge one region at a time every hour, so the edges that are still warm never go cold.
Use new versioned URLs, move pages over gradually and add an origin shield
quiz.explanation: A mass purge turns every edge into a miss at once. Versioned URLs let the change roll out at a pace the origin can handle, and a shield collapses many edge misses into one fetch.
